item.title: China and Germany should deepen cooperation amid economic uncertainty
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-27
BERLIN, Oct. 27 (Xinhua) -- As two major economies with close business ties and complementary strengths, China and Germany have much to gain from deeper engagement and collaboration. German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier's state visit to China, the first in nearly eight years, offers an opportunity to strengthen the foundation of China-Germany economic cooperation and explore new avenues for mutually beneficial development. For Germany, China is seen as a partner in addressing global challenges and a competitor in economic and trade affairs. Concerns over industrial competition and trade imbalances have fueled calls for a tougher approach toward China. Yet these challenges should not overshadow the broader benefits of bilateral economic ties. Trade between the two countries reflects their respective strengths, market demands and business choices. Rather than letting competition undermine cooperation, both sides stand to gain by addressing the concerns through dialogue. Investment figures offer a telling illustration. According to an analysis published by the German Economic Institute, German companies invested around 5.6 billion euros (about 6.5 billion U.S. dollars) in China in the first half of 2026, roughly one-third more than that in the same period a year earlier. A survey by the German Chamber of Commerce in China, cited in the analysis, found that more than 85 percent of German companies operating in China intended to maintain or expand their presence, while more than half planned to increase investment. For German companies, investing in China offers more than access to a large market. China's fast-evolving industrial landscape and strong innovation capabilities also offer opportunities to test new technologies, improve products and respond more quickly to changing market demands. The expertise gained in China can, in turn, help German companies strengthen competitiveness at home and in global markets. This makes a continued presence in China a strategic business choice, not simply a means of expanding sales. Steinmeier's planned visit to Volkswagen's technology center in Hefei, east China's Anhui Province, offers a concrete example of this cooperation. The center integrates vehicle development, component R&D, procurement and testing, enabling Volkswagen to develop and validate vehicles locally and shorten time to market by around 30 percent, according to the German carmaker. These business realities also offer a practical lesson for policymakers: competition need not come at the expense of cooperation. Siemens CEO Roland Busch told German newspaper Welt am Sonntag in August that Chinese companies had become highly capable competitors, citing strong engineering teams, innovative products and rapid adoption of new technologies, including AI. He cautioned against using tariffs to shield industries from competition. BMW CEO Milan Nedeljkovic likewise opposed heightening trade tensions in an interview published by Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung last month, saying, "Nobody is interested in an escalation," and calling for dialogue to resolve trade disputes. The interests of German companies in China reflect a broader reality: China and Germany's economic ties are deeply embedded in each other's industrial development. China has been Germany's largest trading partner in nine of the past 10 years, and the relationship extends well beyond the exchange of finished goods to manufacturing, research and investment. For many businesses in both countries, cooperation across these areas helps them innovate, compete and reach global markets. Preserving and deepening these links is therefore not just about sustaining trade flows, but also about creating new opportunities for both economies to grow. The stakes extend beyond bilateral trade. As the world's second- and third-largest economies, China and Germany, which are all-around strategic partners, share an interest in global economic stability, climate mitigation and multilateral cooperation. As protectionism and uncertainty rattle global supply chains, the two countries can ease the strain by keeping economic channels open, addressing trade concerns through dialogue and working under the auspices of the World Trade Organization. A more stable and balanced economic relationship would benefit businesses and consumers in both nations while supporting broader global growth. Steinmeier's visit offers an opportunity to consolidate mutual trust, strengthen mutual understanding and maintain the momentum of practical cooperation. In a world of growing uncertainty, a stable and constructive China-German relationship can bolster global economic growth and help create a more predictable international environment. ■

item.title: China brings legacy of Tokyo Trial to UN Headquarters with exhibition marking 80th anniversary
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-27
People view exhibits at an exhibition marking the 80th anniversary of the opening of the Tokyo Trial at the UN Headquarters in New York, Oct. 26, 2026. An exhibition marking the 80th anniversary of the opening of the Tokyo Trial opened at UN Headquarters in New York on Monday. Titled "Justice and Peace for All Humanity," the exhibition features historical photographs, archival documents and publications on the investigation and prosecution of Japanese war crimes during World War II. (Xinhua/Zhang Fengguo) UNITED NATIONS, Oct. 26 (Xinhua) -- An exhibition marking the 80th anniversary of the opening of the Tokyo Trial opened at UN Headquarters in New York on Monday. Titled "Justice and Peace for All Humanity," the exhibition features historical photographs, archival documents and publications on the investigation and prosecution of Japanese war crimes during World War II. "The Tokyo Trial cements the post-war world order, upholds fairness and justice, and advances international rule of law. It is a landmark victory of peace over war, civilization over barbarism, and justice over evil, with far-reaching political and historical significance," said Fu Cong, China's permanent representative to the United Nations, at the opening ceremony. "The Tokyo Trial put Japanese militarism in the dock. It's essential for Japan to bear in mind what is at the core of the trial, make a clean break with militarism, and commit itself to peace once and for all," he said. "Regrettably, right-wing forces in Japan keep questioning the legitimacy of the Tokyo Trial under various pretexts, and try to gloss over Japan's history of aggression. From worshiping Class-A war criminals to hollowing out the pacifist Constitution, from easing controls on arms exports to lifting the ban on the right to collective self-defense, Japan is going further away from the Tokyo Trial and tearing up its 'pacifist' rulebook." "History, if not forgotten, can serve as a guide for the future," said Fu. "We need to guard against rising neo-militarism, and together uphold the post-war order and international peace and security." Qi Dahai, director-general of the Department of Treaty and Law of China's Foreign Ministry, Zhou Feng, curator of the Memorial Hall of the Victims in Nanjing Massacre by Japanese Invaders, and officials from Russia and the Democratic People's Republic of Korea addressed the opening ceremony. Permanent representatives to the United Nations from Spain, Nicaragua and other countries attended the ceremony. Speakers highlighted the Tokyo Trial's role in upholding peace through the rule of law and bringing Japan's wartime aggression to justice. They stressed the need to learn from history, remember the suffering caused by war, and work together to prevent the resurgence of militarism and aggression. Organized by China's Permanent Mission to the United Nations, the exhibition is being held during the UN International Law Week. ■ People view exhibits at an exhibition marking the 80th anniversary of the opening of the Tokyo Trial at the UN Headquarters in New York, Oct. 26, 2026. item.title: Xinhua Commentary: Washington's proposed new China curbs could deal costly blow for U.S. businesses
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-27
BEIJING, Oct. 27 (Xinhua) -- The U.S. government's latest proposed rules on outbound investment in China are set to tighten the screws on American businesses yet again. Far from protecting U.S. interests, this move politicizes normal business activity, undermines market principles and fuels uncertainty in China-U.S. economic relations. The U.S. Treasury's proposal to add biotechnology to its outbound investment restrictions on China, alongside curbs on supercomputing and hypersonic technologies, marks another potential expansion of Washington's sweeping investment controls. Fundamentally, the proposed rules run counter to the important consensus reached by the two heads of state. Since the 2023 executive order targeting semiconductors, quantum computing and AI, Washington's approach has remained consistent: impeding China's technological advance. Ironically, biotechnology is where both sides share huge mutual benefits. One-third of the world's innovative drugs in development come from China. In 2025, overseas licensing deals for Chinese innovative drugs reached a historic high of more than 130 billion U.S. dollars, according to China's Ministry of Industry and Information Technology. Major U.S. drugmakers, including Pfizer and Bristol Myers Squibb, have struck multibillion-dollar deals with Chinese biotech firms in 2026, while the U.S. pharmaceutical industry has repeatedly lobbied against stringent investment restrictions. According to the U.S.-China Business Council, 95 percent of respondents to the council consider China "somewhat to very important" for them to stay competitive globally. Washington's restrictions risk undermining the commercial partnerships that American companies see as vital to their competitiveness and depriving them of access to one of the world's most dynamic markets. China remains a magnet for foreign investors. The Ministry of Commerce revealed that China had registered 33.8-percent growth in foreign direct investment (FDI) in high-tech industries during the first nine months of this year. As capital flows into China, U.S. investors constrained by Washington's red tape risk watching valuable opportunities slip away. Biotechnology sits at the heart of global public health. Combating pandemics, advancing breakthroughs in oncology and developing vaccines against infectious diseases all demand pooled scientific data, shared clinical trial networks and cross-border talent flows. By lumping biotech into its national security basket, Washington conflates life-saving medical innovation with the so-called strategic competition. As the world's two largest economies and permanent members of the UN Security Council, China and the United States bear shared global responsibilities to advance health security for all. Unilateral restrictive measures go against the trend of the times and run counter to the due responsibilities of major countries. Time and again, history has shown that the China-U.S. economic relationship is rooted in mutual benefit and win-win cooperation. It must not be derailed by the politicization of economic ties or overstretching of national security concerns. Pressure from Washington will not stop China from moving forward and delivering its opening-up commitment. China will closely follow further developments in the issue and reserves the right to take corresponding measures. It is time for Washington to listen to its own business community and recalibrate its approach along rational and market-oriented lines. Pressure from Washington will only serve to make it very hard for American firms to advance in collaboration with their Chinese peers. ■

item.title: Multinational executives, business delegates seek China opportunities
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-27
TIANJIN, Oct. 27 (Xinhua) -- Bernd Einmeier's recent visit to Tianjin, a port city in northern China, allowed him to see China's development and transformation firsthand. "This is exactly what is important to me: to meet my Chinese friends, to learn from China, to take the best out of China and bring it to German society, and to talk in Germany about China's benefits and Chinese culture," said Einmeier, president of the German-Chinese Association for Economy, Education and Culture. Einmeier was among more than 300 business representatives and other guests from over 30 countries and regions who participated in the 2026 Multinational Enterprises Visit to Tianjin last week. Representing 240 companies, institutions and industry organizations, participants were divided into six groups to explore business opportunities during the three-day event. About 60 percent of the participating companies are Fortune Global 500 firms, hidden champions or industry leaders. They visited industrial parks, businesses and port facilities, focusing on areas including advanced manufacturing, sustainable development, scientific and technological innovation, and international cooperation. Amid global economic uncertainty, multinational companies increasingly seek stable markets, sound business environments, and opportunities for long-term cooperation. China remains a key destination that offers these advantages. According to the Ministry of Commerce, China's foreign direct investment (FDI) equity stock reached 26.8 trillion yuan (about 4 trillion U.S. dollars) in 2025, ranking second globally and marking six consecutive years of growth. One stop on the tour was Flender Ltd., China. Established in Tianjin in 1996 by Germany's Flender, it now operates 19 sales, maintenance and service branches across China. After learning about the company's expansion in China, Larissa Einmeier, project manager at ThinkTank Networks GmbH & Co. KG, said China's rapid development offers abundant opportunities and considerable room for cooperation between German and Chinese businesses. Milton Isidoro, branch manager at VTXRM Chengdu, said his company has operated in China for roughly 10 years and he hopes to explore further opportunities in Tianjin. "There's a very big leasing market and financial market in Tianjin with a lot of companies," Isidoro said. At a circular economy demonstration base operated by the China Resources Recycling Group, industrial materials that had completed their original service life are recycled and reused. Rolf Demmler, general manager of the China branch of the German Sustainable Building Council, spent a long time studying a diagram illustrating the circulation of resources. "I could see China's determination to promote resource recycling and develop a greener economy," Demmler said. China and Germany have considerable potential to cooperate in green industries and sustainable development, he added, noting that the two sides could strengthen exchanges in technology and expertise and pursue joint projects to promote the practical application of green technologies. In recent years, China has accelerated breakthroughs in fields such as artificial intelligence (AI), continued to attract innovation resources, and strengthened its technological capabilities, drawing growing interest from international partners. Jordina Torrents Barrena, senior AI manager and principal AI architect at HP Inc., was impressed by the spirit of innovation in China. "What is impressive here is not only the hardware, but also the software," Barrena said, adding that countries should emphasize collaboration in technology development. Peter Tensen, founder & CEO of GlobalTech IP, brought two delegations to Tianjin, one focused on robotics and the other on AI-driven healthcare and life sciences. "We look forward to identifying the right partners here and combining international technologies with local industrial demand and research capabilities to turn more ideas into practical projects," Tensen said. The event saw the signing of a number of new foreign-invested projects. Multinational companies stepped up investment in areas like high-end manufacturing and biomedicine. Framework agreements on international trade and supply chain cooperation were also signed, while a number of major projects in energy, infrastructure and the circular economy under the Belt and Road Initiative were launched. "China's pace of development and vitality are astonishing," said Kurucz Erika, sales director at PraziTech Kft. from Hungary, who visited China for the first time. "I have seen unlimited possibilities. The door to cooperation is certainly open." ■

item.title: China's industrial profits post strong growth on electronics, high-tech gains
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-27
BEIJING, Oct. 27 (Xinhua) -- China's major industrial firms posted strong profit growth in the first nine months of 2026, driven by robust gains in the electronics industry and high-tech manufacturing, official data showed Tuesday. Profits of major industrial firms with an annual main business revenue of at least 20 million yuan (about 2.98 million U.S. dollars) rose 15.5 percent year on year during the January-September period, maintaining double-digit growth since the beginning of the year, according to the National Bureau of Statistics (NBS). In September alone, industrial profits at those firms increased 14.4 percent year on year, with the growth rate up 10.2 percentage points from August. NBS statistician Yu Weining attributed the overall profit growth to intensified macroeconomic policy support, steady industrial production and accelerated development of new quality productive forces. The electronics industry emerged as a key growth driver, with profits doubling from a year earlier and contributing 9.6 percentage points to the overall increase in industrial profits. Driven by demand for AI computing power and advanced memory technologies, profits in electronic specialty materials manufacturing surged 220 percent, while those in semiconductor discrete device manufacturing rose 51.7 percent. Meanwhile, profits in high-tech manufacturing surged 52 percent year on year, outpacing the overall industrial average by 36.5 percentage points. In the first three quarters, high-tech manufacturing accounted for 25.5 percent of the total profits generated by China's major industrial firms, up 6.2 percentage points from a year earlier. As high-end manufacturing continues to advance and new quality productive forces take shape at a faster pace, China's industrial sector is steadily shifting toward a more advanced and innovation-driven structure, Yu noted. Tuesday's data came as China's 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-2030) highlights the development of a modern industrial system anchored by advanced manufacturing. The country will move to upgrade traditional sectors to the mid-to-high end of the value chain, nurture emerging industries, and make forward-looking plans for industries of the future, according to the development blueprint. Looking ahead, whether industrial profits can sustain robust growth will largely depend on how effectively the momentum in high-tech manufacturing spreads across broader industrial supply chains and whether stronger domestic demand can further support a recovery in profitability among midstream and downstream industries, analysts noted. Wen Bin, chief economist at China Minsheng Bank, said industrial profit growth could face near-term pressure before stabilizing in the fourth quarter, supported by recovering prices and continued strength in certain high-growth industries. He noted that the rollout of 800 billion yuan in new policy-based financial instruments, together with major infrastructure projects and urban renewal initiatives, could stimulate demand for electronic information products, electrical machinery, high-end equipment and certain raw materials. Meanwhile, continued global investment in AI infrastructure is expected to support China's electronics and equipment manufacturing supply chains, while exports of new energy vehicles, energy storage systems and power equipment are likely to remain resilient, Wen said. However, tightening global monetary conditions, uncertainty surrounding U.S. trade policies, geopolitical tensions and energy price fluctuations could weigh on external demand and corporate costs, he cautioned. ■

item.title: China, Europe drive deeper automotive cooperation
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-26
* Chinese cars are gaining popularity across Europe, offering competitive specifications at attractive prices. * Luis Murias, general manager of Spanish automotive data platform DAT, attributes the success of Chinese cars to multiple factors, including "industrial restructuring, commitment, overall quality improvement, competitive features and warranty, and progress in safety standards." BRUSSELS, Oct. 26 (Xinhua) -- In October, Stellantis began producing the Leapmotor B10 at its Zaragoza facility in Spain through its partnership with Chinese electric vehicle (EV) maker Leapmotor. The factory had been running at roughly half capacity, a far cry from its peak output of about 470,000 vehicles in 2019. Stellantis needed to fill its production lines; Leapmotor needed a European base. Neither side called it a favor. The arrangement exemplifies deepening cooperation between China and Europe in the automotive industry, fueled by consumer demand and manufacturers' commercial calculations alike. Analysts say this industrial partnership is more than a stopgap measure, with considerable potential to deliver mutual benefits. CONSUMER VERDICT Chinese cars are gaining popularity across Europe, offering competitive specifications at attractive prices. Chinese brands have targeted a segment that legacy automakers have been slow to serve: drivers who previously owned BMWs, Mercedes-Benzes or Range Rovers. According to one dealership in West London, about three in five buyers of Chinese cars previously owned a luxury brand. Luis Murias, general manager of Spanish automotive data platform DAT, attributes the success of Chinese cars to multiple factors, including "industrial restructuring, commitment, overall quality improvement, competitive features and warranty, and progress in safety standards." A May survey of young Italian consumers by consulting and market research firm Arete Methodos found that 53 percent of respondents are most attracted by the combination of technological features and product quality of Chinese cars -- outnumbering the 43 percent who cite their competitive prices as decisive. In recent years, Chinese car makers have accelerated localization. Ten European production plans have been announced since September 2023, advisory company AutoMotion reported, including BYD's first European plant in Szeged, Hungary and SAIC's 200 million-euro (222.7 million U.S. dollars) factory in Spain's Galicia. SUPPLY-SIDE LOGIC Lithium iron phosphate (LFP) -- a cheaper, longer-lasting battery chemistry that underpins most affordable EVs -- is forecast to rise from around 10 percent of the European battery market today to between 40 and 60 percent by 2030, yet Europe has no operational plants to make it. In September, Gotion High-tech, a Chinese battery manufacturer, agreed to invest around 1.1 billion euros (about 1.23 billion dollars) for a 49 percent stake in Volkswagen's battery-cell plant in Sagunto, Spain. The partnership reflects a complementary division of role. Gotion contributes LFP technology, manufacturing processes and raw material supply chains. PowerCo, Volkswagen's battery subsidiary, brings its European industrial footprint, logistics and regulatory expertise. Javier Rivera, chief financial officer of PowerCo Battery Spain, described the relationship as having evolved "from supplier to technology partner and now to industrial partner." Michael Schumann, chairman of the Board of the German Federal Association for Economic Development and Foreign Trade, told Xinhua that German companies remain active in China. A May 2026 flash survey by the German Chamber of Commerce in China found that the share of companies planning to increase their investments in China over the next two years reached its highest level since 2023. He also pointed to a remarkable shift: German headquarters are increasingly learning from their Chinese operations, not the other way around. "Today, the transformation of the automotive industry, particularly the shift towards electric mobility and software-defined vehicles, is creating new forms of competition and cooperation between German and Chinese companies," Schumann added. "No single country has ever been able to dominate or capture the entire market. As a leading technology company, BYD will bring relevant technologies to Europe," said BYD Executive Vice President Li Ke. "We will grow here and help the local supply chain transition to next-generation suppliers, making important contributions to the local economy." REBALANCING THROUGH COMPLEMENTARITY The automotive sector attracted more Chinese Foreign Direct Investment in 2025 than any other industry in Europe. Investments in the sector totaled 7.6 billion euros (8.5 billion dollars), with 93 percent of them focused on the EV supply chain, according to a report by Rhodium Group and MERICS. "Europe has a great tradition in design," Andrea Levy, president of the Turin Auto Show, told Xinhua, adding that cooperation can combine different strengths and contribute to better vehicles. Industry insiders believe that the pairing is no temporary arrangement. "China Speed is not a cultural phenomenon, but the result of clear decisions regarding product design, portfolio complexity, and the supplier base," said Oliver Knapp, a partner at global management consultancy Roland Berger. "And that is precisely why parts of it can also be implemented in Europe." Alexandre Marian, a partner at AlixPartners, depicted the Stellantis-Leapmotor deal as a "reverse joint venture," in which European manufacturers seek alliances to learn Chinese EV know-how. "If our (Stellantis and Leapmotor) partnership is the strategy, Zaragoza is the proof that we can combine global technology, competitiveness and European industrial capabilities," said Stellantis representative Silvia Vernetti.■

item.title: How a ruling party rules itself -- CPC's perspective
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-26
BEIJING, Oct. 26 (Xinhua) -- With more than 100 million members and the responsibility of governing a country of over 1.4 billion people, the Communist Party of China (CPC) faces an enduring task: identifying and addressing issues within its own ranks. The task has taken on fresh relevance as the CPC prepares to convene the fifth plenary session of its 20th Central Committee in Beijing on Monday. The four-day meeting is scheduled to deliberate on a draft decision on several major issues on persistently advancing full and rigorous Party self-governance. As Chinese President Xi Jinping, also general secretary of the CPC Central Committee, has pointed out, the CPC's full and rigorous self-governance is a great practice in the Party's self-reform in the new era, and has created a new frontier in its self-reform. WHY PERSISTENT SELF-REFORM? At a gathering marking the CPC's 105th founding anniversary in July, Xi said the Party focuses on self-strengthening and always brims with vigor and vitality, referring to it as one of its fine qualities with no parallel among other political parties and political forces. In its pursuit of a better life for the Chinese people, the Party has addressed development challenges through comprehensively deepening reform, while pursuing self-reform to enhance its governing capacity. Since the reform and opening-up in 1978, China has undergone profound transformations. Having achieved tremendous success from humble beginnings, reform efforts have now entered a "deep-water zone." Xi once compared the remaining difficult reforms as "tough bones that are hard to chew." As reforms have advanced into more complex stages, the CPC views full and rigorous governance of the Party as an essential guarantee. Under the banner of self-reform, the CPC has made persistent efforts to improve Party conduct, build a clean government and fight corruption. Haris Bilal Malik, a research fellow at the Institute of Strategic Studies Islamabad in Pakistan, said the CPC's approach treated self-reform as a continuing responsibility of the governing organization. Internal inspections, disciplinary supervision and anti-corruption measures were intended to identify organizational weaknesses, enforce standards of conduct and strengthen policy implementation, he said. Helga Zepp-LaRouche, founder and president of the Schiller Institute, linked the CPC's concept of self-reform to the Confucian tradition of lifelong learning and self-improvement. She said improving governance capacity required a political culture within the Party that was oriented toward serving the people. Volker Tschapke, honorary president of Germany's Prussian Society, said the CPC's efforts went beyond short-term campaigns, reflecting a commitment to continuous self-examination. "This is not for show, this is character," he told Xinhua. HOW DOES OVERSIGHT BECOME ROUTINE? A central question is how self-reform efforts can bring about lasting changes in how officials and institutions operate. The central Party leadership's eight-point decision on improving work conduct, adopted in December 2012, set out rules governing research tours, meetings, documentation and other official duties. Its implementation has targeted problems ranging from the misuse of public funds for holiday gifts to misconduct outside working hours, with regulations, inspections and disciplinary measures reinforcing compliance. Anti-corruption efforts have also continued. China's top anti-graft authorities filed cases against 181 officials directly administered by the Organization Department of the Central Committee of the CPC in 2025, according to the work report of the fifth plenary session of the 20th Central Commission for Discipline Inspection. The work report also revealed that discipline inspection and supervisory authorities filed more than 1 million cases in 2025 and placed 47,000 individuals under detention. A total of 983,000 people received Party disciplinary or administrative punishment. Some 26,000 individuals voluntarily surrendered. Pavel Troshchinsky, a lead researcher at the Russian Academy of Sciences' Institute of China and Contemporary Asia, said China's anti-corruption efforts had moved from "paper requirements" to "real action." He highlighted the CPC's emphasis on ensuring that officials dare not, cannot and will not engage in corruption, combining punishment, institutional restraints and stronger ethical awareness. The CPC has also institutionalized regular inspections to assess whether Party organizations are implementing central decisions, exercising power properly and fulfilling their responsibilities. Inspection teams identify problems and provide feedback, while the organizations concerned must take corrective action under follow-up supervision. In 2025, the fifth and sixth rounds of inspections under the 20th CPC Central Committee were carried out in succession, completing full coverage of all provincial-level regions. The emphasis on corrective action can also be seen in China's environmental governance. Central environmental inspections examine whether local Party committees and governments are fulfilling their environmental protection responsibilities. Following the first round of inspections, which covered all 31 provincial-level regions by the end of 2017, inspection teams conducted a major follow-up review in 2018, covering 20 regions in two batches. Regulations issued in 2025 also provide for follow-up reviews of corrective action when necessary. In south China's Guangdong Province, inspectors found in 2018 that efforts to tackle pollution in the Lianjiang River had made insufficient progress. The findings prompted local authorities to accelerate wastewater treatment projects and tighten controls on industrial discharges. The river's water quality has since improved through sustained cleanup efforts. HOW DOES DISCIPLINE SHAPE DEVELOPMENT? The effects of discipline and oversight extend beyond official conduct to the management of public resources and the implementation of development policies. Efforts to tackle corruption and misconduct in school meal programs offer an example. In 2025, disciplinary and supervisory authorities across China handled 61,000 cases involving corruption and misconduct in such programs, with 35,000 people receiving Party disciplinary or administrative sanctions, according to a report published in February 2026. The authorities also pushed for tighter oversight of school meal funds, procurement and food safety. Waleed Gaballah, a member of the Egyptian Association for Political Economy, Statistics and Legislation, said full and rigorous Party self-governance could strengthen fiscal discipline by curbing the misuse of public funds, reducing waste and improving the implementation of development projects. Emmanuel Matambo, research director of the Center for Africa-China Studies at the University of Johannesburg, said China's experience highlighted the importance of combining development commitments with the ability to recognize shortcomings and correct mistakes. Drawing on China's economic transformation and poverty reduction achievements, he emphasized that governing parties must ensure their policies deliver tangible benefits to the public. Tschapke drew on his visits to China to describe the changes he had witnessed in rural communities and infrastructure. "I have seen with my own eyes what has been achieved: how villages have blossomed through targeted poverty alleviation, how rural areas have found new hope, how high-speed rail connects people and hearts," he said. He associated those changes with the CPC's emphasis on public welfare and its efforts to ensure that resources reach the grassroots. Ruslan Yesin, head of the Department of Comprehensive Chinese Studies at Belarusian State University, attributed the CPC's governance achievements to its combination of long-term planning and pragmatic implementation, commitment to mutually beneficial international cooperation, and people-centered approach to development. Yesin said China's experience offers valuable lessons for the Global South in sustaining steady growth, improving livelihoods and enhancing the capacity for independent development. ■

item.title: Xi leads CPC to advance full, rigorous self-governance
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-26
BEIJING, Oct. 26 (Xinhua) -- The Communist Party of China (CPC) Central Committee on Monday started a four-day plenary session in Beijing, which focuses on strengthening Party self-governance. This marks the latest move by the Party Central Committee with Xi Jinping at its core to strengthen the Party through full and rigorous self-governance. Xi, general secretary of the CPC Central Committee, has emphasized that exercising full and rigorous self-governance is an enduring task for the Party. "One has to be very strong if he wants to strike the iron," Xi said shortly after his election to the post of general secretary of the CPC Central Committee in November 2012. He later warned at a group study session of the Political Bureau of the CPC Central Committee that if corruption is allowed to grow unchecked, "it could spell the end of both the Party and the state." As China entered the new era, the CPC, the largest governing party in the world, faced unprecedented challenges in ensuring reform, development and stability, and addressing problems and risks confronting the nation. Xi has stressed that China's success hinges on the Party, and has made clear that the CPC must continuously strengthen itself through self-governance. In 2014, he explicitly put forward the concept of "exercising full and rigorous Party self-governance" as part of the Party's four-pronged governing strategy, alongside building a moderately prosperous society in all respects, deepening reform and advancing law-based governance. He has made full and rigorous Party self-governance a long-term strategy, as he considers it vital to the Party's long-term governance, the country's enduring stability, and the people's happiness and well-being. BREAK NEW GROUND In December 2012, Xi began strengthening Party self-governance by introducing a code of conduct that became known as the "eight-point rules." It established regulations for Party leaders regarding research tours, meetings, documentation, and other official duties, cracking down on lavish banquets, red carpet events, pomp, entourages, unnecessary meetings, and luxury perks that had once been regarded by some as typical symbols of power. Its implementation has helped curb longstanding malpractices, with effects extending beyond Party and government offices to wider society. "The eight-point rules have indeed brought about fundamental changes over the years," Xi said last year, when the Party launched a campaign to reinforce this code of conduct and consolidate the improvements it had brought about. Xi also launched an unprecedented anti-corruption storm that has swept every corner of public office, netting both high-ranking "tigers" and lower-level "flies." Some of the most senior officials -- including former members of the Political Bureau and its Standing Committee, top military brass, and retirees who left their leading positions years ago -- have been brought to justice. The anti-corruption campaign has continued unabated, with Xi stressing that the fight is an ongoing endeavor. In 2025 alone, 115 officials at ministerial level or above were placed under investigation, while 627,000 people were disciplined in cases involving misconduct and corruption that affect the people's immediate interests. The same year, China also opened investigations into more than 500 cases of cross-border corruption. At a plenary session of the CPC's top disciplinary body early this year, Xi again warned that corruption remains a problem that arises all too easily and frequently. "We must see the fight against corruption through to the end, no matter how great the resistance or how high the cost," he said. "No one who engages in corruption will be shown leniency, regardless of who they are, how high their rank or how great their contributions." EFFECTIVE APPROACHES To strengthen full and rigorous Party self-governance, it is imperative to uphold the Party's overall leadership. Over the past 14 years, the Party's leadership has been further affirmed in both the Party Constitution and the country's Constitution. Central commissions have been established to oversee key areas including reform, national security, cyberspace affairs, and financial and economic affairs. Working mechanisms for central decision-making and coordinating bodies have also been strengthened. Strengthening theoretical education is another approach. With Xi at the helm, the CPC has launched nine Party-wide major education campaigns. The latest one, launched in February this year, prodded Party members to fix their mindset regarding governance performance, aiming to stamp out the tendency among some officials to sacrifice public well-being in seeking to polish their performance records. This campaign built on the gains of previous ones on Party discipline and implementing the eight-point rules, among others, to advance the Party's self-governance. These efforts have gone hand in hand with institution-building. Under Xi's watch, the Party and state oversight systems have been improved. The National Commission of Supervision and local supervisory commissions were established to bring everyone in public office, regardless of Party membership, under supervision. And Xi has made discipline inspections a key instrument of intra-Party oversight. The inspection system allows higher-level Party authorities to send teams to examine how officials exercise power and carry out the central leadership's policies. Inspectors interview officials and members of the public, review documents and receive complaints. They report their findings to Party authorities. After each round of inspections launched by the Party Central Committee, Xi reviewed the reports in detail, assessed the problems uncovered and pushed for further improvements in inspection work. Since 2012, the Party has also formulated or revised an unprecedented number of internal regulations, building a comprehensive framework of rules to confine power in "a cage of institutions." Noting the progress, Xi also warned that in some localities, rules were poorly enforced while "hidden rules" prevailed. He stressed that regulations must become "high-voltage lines" and that power must be exercised transparently, leaving no room for such hidden rules. All these mechanisms are part of the integrated efforts to ensure officials, in Xi's words, "do not have the audacity, opportunity, or desire to become corrupt." LEADING MODERNIZATION DRIVE Full and rigorous Party self-governance serves a broader purpose: strengthening the Party's capacity to lead China's modernization drive. "To successfully achieve the goals and tasks of the 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-2030), it is imperative to focus on enhancing the ability and competence of the Party in leading economic and social development," Xi told senior provincial- and ministerial-level officials attending a study session at the Party School of the CPC Central Committee earlier this year. He urged Party officials to become more capable of pursuing high-quality development, serving the people, and guarding against and defusing risks. China has entered a critical period for achieving the goal of basically realizing modernization by 2035, and still faces rising uncertainty abroad and mounting challenges at home. At such critical junctures, strong Party leadership is vital to chart the course. All Party members, Xi said, must remain true to the Party's original aspiration and mission, and lead the nation to "create new historic glories." ■
